news.title: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess
news.title_en: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess
news.author: Will Knight
news.article_content:
Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.

But just as he’s leaving, the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia, where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.

“Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.

Already, competitors have started to move in.

Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.

Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.

Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.

Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025.

And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes.

Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.

In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.

While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.

Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.

Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms.

Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.

Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.

Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.

Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes.

But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.

But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.

Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.

Every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he says. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.

Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, says Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the company’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.

“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he says.

news.article_content_zh:
英伟达在推动人工智能淘金热中发挥了关键作用，这在很大程度上要归功于其最近被罢免的首席执行官黄仁勋。黄仁勋是预见技术变革的大师，他比大多数人更早地投资芯片来训练人工智能。

但就在他离开时，该公司的竞争对手越来越多，他们采用了一系列先进的新技术。对于目前由首席财务官科莱特·克雷斯(Colette Kress)接任的英伟达来说，时机并不好。

一家大型人工智能公司的首席执行官表示：“今天出售的所有产品都是两三年前设计的。”为了避免损害业务关系，他不愿透露姓名。这位首席执行官表示，克雷斯或任何永久取代她的人都必须制定芯片行业两年后的发展方向。

竞争对手已经开始介入。

根据 Silicon Analysis 的数据，Nvidia 在人工智能加速器市场占据主导地位，占据了 80% 的销售额。长期以来的宿敌AMD现在正在齐心协力打造有竞争力的AI芯片。其市场份额已从 2022 年的 2% 攀升至 2026 年的 7% 至 10%。

美国大型云计算公司——谷歌、亚马逊和微软——都在开发更专业的芯片来支持人工智能模型的训练和服务。每个人都获得了相似的收益。这些公司正在设计自己的芯片，以降低成本并获得一定程度的独立于 Nvidia 的地位。

几家初创公司现在提供更专业的芯片，有望对 Nvidia 的核心产品进行改进。例如，Cerebras 销售旨在为巨型人工智能模型提供动力的大型产品。 AMD 最近收购了 Taalas，这家公司将模型的权重刻录到硅片中，从而使计算变得非常高效。然而，使用这些芯片需要重写大量代码，才能使它们与尖端的人工智能模型一起工作。

跟踪芯片行业的公司 MoorInStrat 的首席分析师帕特里克·穆尔黑德 (Patrick Moorhead) 表示，人工智能代理的兴起使得推理或运行已经训练过的模型变得更加重要。与云超大规模企业和初创公司相比，英伟达在这个领域的优势较小。然而，Nvidia 确实于 2025 年 12 月收购了一家生产专用芯片的初创公司 Grok。

摩尔黑德表示，由于人工智能助手和代理的兴起，对通用中央处理器（CPU）的需求也不断增长，而英伟达在这一领域几乎没有竞争。

得益于黄仁勋的远见，英伟达在人工智能领域仍然保持着巨大的领先优势。黄先生于 1993 年与他人共同创立了该公司，为 PC 设计图形芯片。 2010 年代中期，他看到了人工智能的前景。他资助了该主题的学术研究，开发了支持人工智能工程的软件，并向实验室和初创公司提供了硬件。

2022年，ChatGPT让AI成为主流，Nvidia芯片销量猛增。该公司的收入从 2022 年 1 月的 269.1 亿美元增至 2026 年 1 月的 2159.4 亿美元。它面临的挑战可能不是存在的，但它们确实会累积起来，尤其是在全球范围内。

尽管英伟达在美国的命运有所上升，但在世界另一个人工智能大市场中国却出现了下滑。华盛顿正试图限制其最先进芯片的使用，而北京则试图发展自己的芯片产业。英伟达不允许在中国销售其最强大的芯片，但它可以销售前几代芯片。根据其备案信息，这些芯片以及非人工智能芯片的销售额在过去一年中翻了一番，但中国目前仅占该公司总收入的 8%，而 2024 年将占 20%。目前尚不清楚有多少出口到其他国家的芯片可能最终进入中国或最终被中国公司远程使用。

多年来一直受到美国制裁的中国科技巨头华为开发了新型超级计算机，可以利用比平常更多的芯片来训练和运行人工智能模型。一些中国人工智能公司，例如拥有世界上最好的开源模型之一的再爱科技，表示他们已经完全使用华为的芯片来训练他们的模型。如果中国的开放式重量模型在其他国家获得关注，它可能会在其他国家为中国芯片创造市场。

黄与中国的往来在他的垮台中发挥了重要作用。他与黄乐（又名爱丽丝·黄）有过一段浪漫关系，黄乐是一家名为 Megaspeed 的新加坡公司的中国高管，美国政府怀疑该公司是中国国家安全部的资产。据报道，Megaspeed 及其子公司已向东南亚进口价值 4.6 至 75 亿美元的 Nvidia 芯片。有报道称，该公司可能已向中国人工智能公司提供了这些芯片的使用权。

It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.

Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.

He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.

Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.

Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.

Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes.

But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.

But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.

Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.

Every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he says. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.

Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, says Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the company’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.

“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he says.

“Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.

Revenue for the three months ended September slid 1% to 30.8 billion yuan ($4.6 billion), in line with the average analyst forecast. Net income came in at 1.4 billion yuan.

China's internet search leader is trying to reclaim its place in a hotly contested AI arena where longtime rivals such as Tencent Holdings Ltd. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. have pulled ahead. Its Ernie model series has fallen out of the top tier and lags upstarts like DeepSeek and Moonshot, while its consumer AI products have yet to catch on. Compounding the slump, Baidu's main online advertising business is losing eyeballs and marketers to newer social apps.

Billionaire founder Robin Li is betting that a surge in autonomous AI agents will create a new ecosystem from which Baidu can reap returns on its cloud computing and chip infrastructure. Its AI-driven business now accounts for more than half of its top line, a trend the company expects to persist. The company last week unveiled a token marketplace that connects idle compute with developers hungry for open-source models — a move aimed at displacing middlemen, known as transfer stations, with accredited providers.

The resource-constrained company lacks the scale to compete with China's tech platforms and the strain is beginning to show as Baidu simultaneously pursues leadership in China's AI, cloud and robotaxi sectors. The potential spinoff and IPO of the Kunlunxin AI chip unit won't improve its earnings prospects, which are highly challenged.

Its chip spinoff Kunlunxin is gearing up for an independent listing in Hong Kong, setting up a showdown against Alibaba's T-Head, which announced a similar move. But Kunlunxin's market debut could slip to next year because of broader market weakness and China's tighter controls on AI funding, Bloomberg News has reported.

Baidu last week released its latest foundation model, Ernie 5.5 Flash Preview, which it positioned for fast inference speeds and competitive pricing.

In autonomous driving, Baidu's Apollo Go robotaxi service now spans more than a score of cities globally, including fully driverless commercial operations in Dubai.

截至 9 月份的三个月收入下滑 1%，至 308 亿元人民币（46 亿美元），与分析师的平均预测一致。净利润为14亿元。

中国互联网搜索领导者正试图在竞争激烈的人工智能领域夺回自己的地位，腾讯控股有限公司和阿里巴巴集团控股有限公司等长期竞争对手已经领先。其Ernie模型系列已跌出顶级，落后于DeepSeek和Moonshot等新贵，而其消费级人工智能产品尚未流行。令业绩下滑雪上加霜的是，百度的主要在线广告业务正在失去眼球和营销人员，转向新的社交应用程序。

百度上周发布了最新的基础模型 Ernie 5.5 Flash Preview，其定位是快速的推理速度和有竞争力的价格。

news.title: Apple Was Late to the Video Podcast Boom. Now It’s Trying to Catch Up.
news.title_en: Apple Was Late to the Video Podcast Boom. Now It’s Trying to Catch Up.

inline_images.caption: Oliver Schusser, an Apple vice president, at right. “We want podcasts to be available wherever people want to enjoy them — the small screens, big screens,” he said. (Caroline Brehman/EPA, via Shutterstock)
inline_images.alt: Oliver Schusser, an Apple vice president, at right. “We want podcasts to be available wherever people want to enjoy them — the small screens, big screens,” he said.

inline_images.caption: Rachel Martin, the host of Wild Card, an NPR podcast.
inline_images.alt: Rachel Martin, the host of Wild Card, an NPR podcast.

news.author: Sapna Maheshwari and Kalley Huang
news.article_content:
Apple helped turbocharge the rise of podcasts two decades ago, but as video podcasts reshape the industry it’s fallen behind competitors like YouTube and Spotify.

Now it’s playing catch up. On Monday, Apple will add a video podcasts section to Apple TV, initially just for testing with developers. They will soon be free to all users even if they don’t pay for Apple’s streaming service and will appear on over one billion devices that have the Apple TV app, including Rokus and smart TVs. Apple also plans to increase the number of video podcasts on its regular Podcasts app, where it introduced video features nine months ago but has been working to bring some of the biggest shows on board.

“We want podcasts to be available wherever people want to enjoy them — the small screens, big screens,” said Oliver Schusser, a vice president at Apple who oversees services including podcasts, television and music. “It’s really about discovery and helping the creators to reach a new audience. We didn’t approach this in a way that would financially benefit us.”

Video podcasts have proliferated in the past few years as audio creators adapted their shows to reach consumers spending more time on video platforms like YouTube. The video format has proved attractive to celebrities, including Amy Poehler, Pete Davidson and Food Network’s Ina Garten. And the trend of “clipping” — creating short buzzy video clips from longer shows to post on social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram — has encouraged creators to add video to their podcasts.

The popularity of video podcasts, driven by YouTube and Spotify, and newer entrants like Hulu and Netflix, has pushed Apple down in the podcast platform rankings. Spotify passed Apple as the top platform among weekly podcast consumers in the United States at the end of 2022, according to survey data from Edison Research at SSRS. YouTube took over the top spot at the end of 2024. In Edison Research’s third-quarter survey, YouTube remained the most popular, followed by Spotify then Apple Podcasts. Netflix was No. 7.

Many in the industry had long awaited Apple’s move.

“It’s super smart that they’ve done it, but it’s after a lot of people in the space wanted them to make it available,” said Megan Lazovick, a vice president at Edison Research.

Apple’s addition of video to its regular app earlier this year has been encouraging, with overall audiences for top shows that added video growing by more than 20 percent on average. That includes shows like IMO with Michelle Obama and Craig Robinson and the comedy podcast Giggly Squad.

Sam Fragoso, the host of the show Talk Easy, had been “eager” for Apple to add video, saying it had doubled the audience of his show, which is also available on Spotify and YouTube.

“It’s so helpful that people can go on their phones, they see a clip on Instagram, TikTok or Twitter and open the Apple app and now watch it on video,” he said. “People are already on their iPhones and they’re used to watching videos on their phones so it was the next logical step.”

Apple’s history may help it catch up to competitors who were earlier to the video podcast boom.

“I love our YouTube audience but it feels not as intentional on that platform — Apple’s where people know where to find their favorite podcasts,” said Rachel Martin, the host of NPR’s Wild Card.

Her show’s audience has grown by more than 60 percent since Apple introduced video, which she called astonishing in an industry where “sometimes it can feel excruciating and really hard to get just another 100 subscribers.”

In 2005, podcasts were viewed as a way for Apple to sell more iPods, the popular audio player that connected to iTunes. (Tech journalists once compared it to a razor company trying to sell more products by distributing free razor blades.) Today, Apple still seems to view video podcasts as a sweetener for devices, including newer products like its iPhone Duo and the upcoming HomeView tablet.

Mr. Schusser said he envisions a future where people can listen to their favorite podcasts as they move through their day.

More than 35 percent of video podcast consumers actively switch between watching and listening to shows in a given month, Apple’s data shows. Some view it as a sign that video podcasts are the future.

“Everything is TV now, which is a little bit heartbreaking for a lifelong audio person to say,” Ms. Martin of NPR said. “I don’t think this is a flash in the pan.”

news.article_content_zh:
二十年前，苹果推动了播客的崛起，但随着视频播客重塑了该行业，它落后于 YouTube 和 Spotify 等竞争对手。

现在它正在迎头赶上。周一，苹果将在 Apple TV 中添加视频播客部分，最初只是为了与开发者进行测试。即使用户不支付苹果的流媒体服务费用，它们很快也将免费提供给所有用户，并将出现在超过 10 亿台装有 Apple TV 应用的设备上，包括 Rokus 和智能电视。苹果还计划增加其常规播客应用程序上的视频播客数量，该应用程序在九个月前引入了视频功能，但一直在努力将一些最大的节目引入其中。

苹果负责播客、电视和音乐等服务的副总裁奥利弗·舒瑟 (Oliver Schusser) 表示：“我们希望人们可以在任何想要享受播客的地方观看播客，无论是小屏幕还是大屏幕。” “这实际上是关于发现并帮助创作者接触新观众。我们并没有以一种能给我们带来经济利益的方式来处理这个问题。”

过去几年，随着音频​​创作者调整自己的节目以吸引在 YouTube 等视频平台上花费更多时间的消费者，视频播客激增。事实证明，这种视频格式对艾米·波勒、皮特·戴维森和食品网络的伊娜·加滕等名人很有吸引力。 “剪辑”的趋势——从较长的节目中创建简短的热门视频剪辑并发布到 TikTok 和 Instagram 等社交媒体平台上——鼓励创作者将视频添加到他们的播客中。

在 YouTube 和 Spotify 以及 Hulu 和 Netflix 等新进入者的推动下，视频播客的流行使得苹果在播客平台排名中下降。根据 SSRS 爱迪生研究中心的调查数据，到 2022 年底，Spotify 超过苹果，成为美国每周播客消费者中排名第一的平台。 YouTube 在 2024 年底占据了榜首。在爱迪生研究公司第三季度的调查中，YouTube 仍然是最受欢迎的，其次是 Spotify，然后是 Apple Podcasts。 Netflix 排名第七。

许多业内人士对苹果的举动期待已久。

爱迪生研究公司副总裁梅根·拉佐维克 (Megan Lazovick) 表示：“他们这样做非常聪明，但这是在该领域的很多人希望他们提供它之后。”

苹果公司今年早些时候在其常规应用程序中添加了视频，这令人鼓舞，添加视频的热门节目的总体观众数量平均增长了 20% 以上。其中包括米歇尔·奥巴马和克雷格·罗宾逊的《IMO》节目以及喜剧播客《Giggly Squad》。

Talk Easy 节目的主持人萨姆·弗拉戈索 (Sam Fragoso) 一直“渴望”苹果添加视频，称这使他的节目的观众人数增加了一倍，该节目也可以在 Spotify 和 YouTube 上观看。

“这非常有帮助，人们可以在手机上看到 Instagram、TikTok 或 Twitter 上的剪辑，然后打开 Apple 应用程序，然后在视频中观看，”他说。 “人们已经在使用 iPhone，并且习惯了在手机上观看视频，因此这是下一个合乎逻辑的步骤。”

苹果的历史可能有助于它赶上较早进入视频播客热潮的竞争对手。

“我喜欢我们的 YouTube 观众，但在这个平台上感觉并不是那么有意为之——人们知道在苹果平台上哪里可以找到他们最喜欢的播客，”NPR 节目 Wild Card 的主持人雷切尔·马丁 (Rachel Martin) 说道。

自从 Apple 推出视频以来，她的节目的观众数量增长了 60% 以上，她称这在一个“有时会让人感到痛苦且很难再获得 100 名订阅者”的行业中令人震惊。

2005 年，播客被视为苹果公司销售更多 iPod（连接 iTunes 的流行音频播放器）的一种方式。 （科技记者曾将其比作一家剃须刀公司，试图通过分发免费剃须刀刀片来销售更多产品。）如今，苹果似乎仍然将视频播客视为设备的甜味剂，包括 iPhone Duo 和即将推出的 HomeView 平板电脑等新产品。

舒瑟先生说，他设想未来人们可以在一天中收听自己喜欢的播客。

Apple 的数据显示，超过 35% 的视频播客消费者在特定月份内主动在观看和收听节目之间切换。一些人认为这标志着视频播客是未来。

“现在一切都是电视，对于一个终生从事音频工作的人来说，这样说有点令人心碎，”NPR 的马丁女士说。 “我不认为这只是昙花一现。”

“Everything is TV now, which is a little bit heartbreaking for a lifelong audio person to say,” Ms. Martin of NPR said. “I don’t think this is a flash in the pan.”

news.author: Laurie Chen and Xiuyuan Ning
news.article_content:
BEIJING, Nov 16 (Reuters) - At a top private school in Beijing, 13-year-old Peng Gaodi has used artificial intelligence to build more than 200 apps, including a homework-submission platform and a secondhand marketplace. He pitches ideas to real investors, idolises Elon Musk and hopes to become a computer scientist.

Around him, classmates program humanoid robots to play soccer, attend coding workshops and train on flight simulators. Posters across the 30-acre (12-hectare) boarding school campus encourage students to "create a virtual world in five minutes with AI vibe coding."

"In the past, if I couldn't solve a problem at home, I'd have to call my teacher, which increases their workload," Peng said. "But now I can just ask AI to help me learn better. It noticeably improved my learning efficiency."

Rare access granted to Reuters at the $39,000-a-year Beijing New Talent Academy offered a window into China's push to weave AI into education. The school, which serves more than 2,000 students, has built its own digital innovation curriculum covering AI, robotics and programming, and developed a classroom AI model incorporating features from popular Chinese systems.

The academy represents the sharp end of a broader transformation. With almost 200 million students enrolled in primary and secondary education, China is undertaking one of the world's largest AI-assisted learning experiments, with the technology increasingly integrated into teaching nationwide.

By 2030, Beijing wants AI literacy to be universal among schoolchildren. Current broad AI education guidelines state that students should progress from understanding basic concepts in their early years to applying advanced tools and critical-thinking skills in complex projects.

A weeks-long Reuters examination, based on school visits, interviews with more than a dozen educators, parents and experts, and a review of more than 100 academic papers and government procurement records, paints one of the most detailed pictures yet of how AI is reshaping Chinese classrooms. It found a sweeping but uneven effort to build a generation of AI-savvy innovators, with little consensus on what AI literacy means, how it should be taught or measured.

China views the technology as central to its economic future and technological rivalry with the United States, hoping early exposure will nurture the homegrown innovation needed for major breakthroughs.

Beijing's state-led push far outpaces efforts in the West. President Xi Jinping has declared AI education fundamental to reform. By contrast, the US relies on decentralized, nonbinding guidance and lacks dedicated funding or state-level teacher standards, according to Stanford University's 2026 AI Index.

A Reuters review of provincial "AI+ education" blueprints reveals a degree of official coordination unseen elsewhere. Nearly half of China's provinces and municipalities have rolled out binding plans. Shanghai mandates at least 30 hours of annual teaching on AI skills per grade, while the Beijing city government plans to integrate AI into student health monitoring, as well as set up 100 AI pilot demonstration schools. Underscoring its importance, regions including Ningxia and Gansu plan to integrate AI literacy directly into high-stakes school entrance exams by 2027.

The documents also offer an early look at more expansive classroom applications. Beyond coding and tutoring, Guizhou is integrating AI facial recognition and behavioral analysis into classrooms, while Shanghai is deploying systems for mental and physical health monitoring. In Yunnan, 14,000 classrooms are slated to have lessons recorded and analysed by AI, turning Chinese schools into a high-stakes testing ground for the opportunities and risks confronting global education.

As AI spreads through Chinese classrooms, many educators are grappling with how to deploy the technology without reinforcing the rote-learning habits policymakers want to move beyond.

Reuters found starkly different approaches across the country. While some schools encourage students like Peng to build and create with AI, others are focused on using the technology to plug gaps in educational resources.

"Implementation is all over the place," said Ted Mo Chen, chief of staff at Chinese education technology startup ClassIn, adding that few schools he had visited had integrated AI into the curriculum effectively.

China's education ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

CLASSROOMS OF THE FUTURE

Headmaster Liu Wei said only a small minority of students at Beijing New Talent Academy would become AI scientists or engineers. For the rest, the objective is to make AI an everyday tool for learning and creating.

Hundreds of kilometres away in rural Anhui province, Funan County Qinqing High School is using the same technology to solve a problem affluent urban areas in China rarely face: a shortage of qualified teachers.

The school's 4,000 pupils, most of them children of migrant workers, learn core subjects through AI-generated lessons, according to headmaster Yang Tianliang. Students follow personalised classes on tablets, with AI agents posing questions rather than providing answers when they struggle.

"An AI agent doesn't suffer from fatigue, and it never makes a student feel stupid for asking a basic question," Yang said.

The school uses popular Chinese AI models from Alibaba's Qwen, ByteDance and Z.AI to generate text, images, interactive lessons and videos. Yang said it had also introduced small-group projects to encourage greater student interaction.

He credited the approach with helping lift university admission rates from below 60% to 90% in recent years, although Reuters could not independently verify the figures. Yang estimated at least 200 other Chinese schools were experimenting with similar systems.

An Alibaba spokesperson said its open-source AI models and Cloud for Youth Programme give students direct access to AI tools and education. ByteDance and Z.AI did not respond to requests for comment.

Schools such as Funan County Qinqing High School offer a glimpse of how quickly AI is spreading through China's education system.

Since 2024, China's education ministry has encouraged schools to introduce AI courses, train teachers and develop pilot programmes. Primary-school pupils are introduced to basic AI tools, while older students learn how AI systems work and apply them to increasingly sophisticated projects.

A Reuters review of more than 100 government procurement documents found authorities committed at least $31 million in the past year to AI classroom equipment, training and teaching platforms.

The true figure is likely far higher, scattered across thousands of local budgets and not officially tallied. Consultancy iResearch estimates 2025 spending on education digitalisation at just under $83 billion, with generative AI projects accounting for 46% of AI education procurement.

AN EXPERIMENT WITHOUT A CLEAR SCORECARD

China has yet to establish a standard framework for measuring AI literacy, leaving schools to experiment and making success difficult to assess.

"Mature, widely adopted assessment rubrics for compulsory school-level AI competency are still being built," said Selena Guo, portfolio lead at research firm China Policy.

Preliminary research into AI's effects on children's learning also offers mixed signals, with some studies suggesting short-term gains while raising questions about longer-term intellectual development.

A recent study examining nearly 27,000 Chinese teenagers found AI adoption was associated with an 18% increase in homework scores but a 20% decline in monthly examination scores within six months, with the biggest declines in social science subjects.

Another nationwide Chinese survey this year involving more than 320,000 pupils reported educational benefits from AI but also concerns about dependence and weaker independent thinking. Students using AI at least three times weekly showed lower memory, comprehension, analytical and creative skills than less frequent users.

The findings do not establish causation but reinforce teacher concerns about cognitive outsourcing, where children increasingly delegate mental tasks to technology rather than develop those skills themselves.

Chen from ClassIn warned that children's thinking processes could be "completely bypassed" if schools failed to prevent them from relying on AI for quick answers.

Chinese academic research reviewed by Reuters also suggested that students in rural areas may be particularly vulnerable to cognitive outsourcing and device addiction.

FINDING THE RIGHT BALANCE

Some educators and parents are already experimenting with safeguards to keep AI from replacing critical thinking.

At Beijing New Talent Academy, Peng said he tries to solve coding problems himself before asking AI for hints rather than complete answers. He said the technology has helped deepen his understanding of maths.

"I think AI is a tool that helps me, not something I depend on."

For Beijing parent Rita Luan, whose 11-year-old daughter attends a leading public school in the capital, the challenge is ensuring that AI strengthens rather than shortcuts learning.

She said her daughter's school still largely teaches AI concepts rather than practical applications, so she supplements lessons at home, teaching her daughter to prompt ByteDance's Doubao chatbot under close supervision.

Her rule: spend 15 minutes trying to solve a difficult maths problem before turning to AI. Days later, Luan asks her to solve the same problem without help.

"The point is to make sure she actually digested the solution," she said.

news.title_zh: 中国部署AI教育普及：国家战略迈向2030
news.summary_zh: 北京新英才学校等基础教育学府全面普及AI生成课程、飞行模拟实验室与机器人训练，各级政府投入逾3100万美元采购AI教学装备，加速迈向2030国家AI教育战略普及
news.article_content_zh:
路透北京11月16日 - 在北京一所顶尖私立学校，13岁的彭高弟利用人工智能开发了200多个应用程序，包括作业提交平台和二手市场。他向真正的投资者推销想法，崇拜埃隆·马斯克，并希望成为一名计算机科学家。

在他周围，同学们编写人形机器人踢足球、参加编程研讨会以及飞行模拟器训练。占地 30 英亩（12 公顷）的寄宿学校校园内张贴的海报鼓励学生“利用 AI 氛围编码在五分钟内创建一个虚拟世界”。

“过去，如果我在家解决不了问题，我就得打电话给老师，这增加了他们的工作量，”彭说。 “但现在我可以要求人工智能帮助我更好地学习。它显着提高了我的学习效率。”

路透社罕见地访问了每年收费 39,000 美元的北京新英才学院，这为了解中国推动人工智能融入教育提供了一个窗口。该校为2000多名学生提供服务，建立了自己的数字创新课程，涵盖人工智能、机器人和编程，并开发了融合中国流行系统特点的课堂人工智能模型。

该学院代表了更广泛变革的尖端。中国有近2亿中小学学生，正在开展世界上最大的人工智能辅助学习实验之一，该技术越来越多地融入全国教学。

北京希望到 2030 年，学童能够普及人工智能知识。目前广泛的人工智能教育指南指出，学生应该从早年理解基本概念发展到在复杂项目中应用先进工具和批判性思维技能。

路透社为期一周的调查基于学校走访、对十几位教育工作者、家长和专家的采访，以及对 100 多篇学术论文和政府采购记录的审查，描绘了迄今为止人工智能如何重塑中国课堂的最详细的画面之一。研究发现，为培养一代精通人工智能的创新者，人们付出了广泛但不均衡的努力，但对于人工智能素养的含义、如何教授或衡量人工智能素养几乎没有达成共识。

中国将这项技术视为其经济未来和与美国技术竞争的核心，希望早期接触能够培育重大突破所需的本土创新。

北京政府主导的推动力度远远超过西方国家。习近平主席宣布人工智能教育是改革的基础。相比之下，根据斯坦福大学的 2026 年人工智能指数，美国依赖分散的、不具约束力的指导，缺乏专用资金或州级教师标准。

路透社对省级“人工智能+教育”蓝图的审查揭示了其他地方未见的官方协调程度。中国近一半的省市已经出台了约束性计划。上海要求每个年级每年至少有30个小时的人工智能技能教学，而北京市政府计划将人工智能融入学生健康监测，并建立100所人工智能试点示范学校。为了强调其重要性，宁夏和甘肃等地区计划到 2027 年将人工智能素养直接纳入高风险的入学考试。

这些文件还提供了对更广泛的课堂应用的早期了解。除了编码和辅导之外，贵州正在将人工智能面部识别和行为分析融入课堂，而上海正在部署心理和身体健康监测系统。在云南，14,000个教室将通过人工智能记录和分析课程，将中国学校变成全球教育面临的机遇和风险的高风险试验场。

随着人工智能在中国课堂上的传播，许多教育工作者正在努力解决如何在不强化政策制定者希望超越的死记硬背习惯的情况下部署该技术。

路透社发现全国各地的做法截然不同。虽然一些学校鼓励像彭这样的学生利用人工智能进行构建和创造，但其他学校则专注于利用该技术来填补教育资源的空白。

中国教育科技初创公司 ClassIn 的幕僚长 Ted Mo Chen 表示：“实施无处不在。”他补充说，他访问过的学校很少有将人工智能有效融入课程的。

中国教育部没有回应置评请求。

刘伟校长表示，北京新英才学院的学生中只有一小部分会成为人工智能科学家或工程师。至于其他方面，我们的目标是让人工智能成为日常学习和创造的工具。

数百公里外的安徽省农村地区，阜南县勤庆中学正在使用相同的技术来解决中国富裕城市地区很少面临的问题：合格教师短缺。

校长杨天亮表示，学校有 4000 名学生，其中大部分是农民工子女，他们通过人工智能生成的课程学习核心科目。学生们在平板电脑上学习个性化课程，人工智能代理会在他们遇到困难时提出问题，而不是提供答案。

杨说：“人工智能代理不会感到疲劳，而且它永远不会让学生因为问一个基本问题而感到愚蠢。”

学校使用阿里巴巴 Qwen、ByteDance 和 Z.AI 等中国流行的人工智能模型来生成文本、图像、互动课程和视频。杨说，学校还引入了小组项目，以鼓励更多的学生互动。

他称赞这种方法近年来帮助大学录取率从 60% 以下提高到 90%，尽管路透社无法独立核实这些数字。杨估计至少还有 200 所其他中国学校正在试验类似的系统。

阿里巴巴发言人表示，其开源人工智能模型和青年云计划让学生可以直接获得人工智能工具和教育。字节跳动和 Z.AI 没有回应置评请求。

阜南县沁青高中等学校让我们得以一窥人工智能在中国教育体系中的传播速度。

自2024年起，中国教育部鼓励学校引进人工智能课程、培训教师并开发试点项目。小学生将学习基本的人工智能工具，而年龄较大的学生将学习人工智能系统的工作原理并将其应用到日益复杂的项目中。

路透社对 100 多份政府采购文件的审查发现，当局在过去一年中为人工智能教室设备、培训和教学平台承诺了至少 3100 万美元。

真实数字可能要高得多，分散在数千个地方预算中并且没有官方统计。艾瑞咨询咨询公司估计，到 2025 年，教育数字化支出将接近 830 亿美元，其中生成式人工智能项目占人工智能教育采购的 46%。

没有明确成绩单的试验

中国尚未建立衡量人工智能素养的标准框架，让学校只能进行实验，也难以评估成功与否。

研究公司 China Policy 的投资组合主管 SelenaGuo 表示：“成熟的、广泛采用的学校必修人工智能能力评估标准仍在制定中。”

关于人工智能对儿童学习影响的初步研究也提供了混合信号，一些研究表明人工智能在短期收益的同时提出了有关长期智力发展的问题。

最近一项对近 27,000 名中国青少年进行的研究发现，人工智能的采用与六个月内家庭作业成绩提高 18% 相关，但每月考试成绩下降 20%，其中社会科学科目下降幅度最大。

今年另一项涉及超过 320,000 名学生的全国性调查报告了人工智能带来的教育益处，但也担心依赖和独立思考能力较弱。每周至少使用人工智能 3 次的学生的记忆力、理解力、分析能力和创造能力低于使用频率较低的学生。

研究结果并没有确定因果关系，但加剧了教师对认知外包的担忧，即孩子们越来越多地将脑力任务委托给技术，而不是自己发展这些技能。

“我认为人工智能是一个帮助我的工具，而不是我所依赖的东西。”

北京家长丽塔·栾 (Rita Luan) 11 岁的女儿就读于首都一所顶尖的公立学校，对于她来说，面临的挑战是确保人工智能加强而不是阻碍学习。

她说，女儿的学校仍然主要教授人工智能概念，而不是实际应用，因此她在家补课，在密切监督下教女儿提示字节跳动的豆宝聊天机器人。

她的规则是：在求助于人工智能之前花 15 分钟尝试解决一道困难的数学问题。几天后，栾要求她在没有帮助的情况下解决同样的问题。

“关键是要确保她真正消化了这个解决方案，”她说。

subheadings: CLASSROOMS OF THE FUTURE
AN EXPERIMENT WITHOUT A CLEAR SCORECARD
FINDING THE RIGHT BALANCE
paragraphs: BEIJING, Nov 16 (Reuters) - At a top private school in Beijing, 13-year-old Peng Gaodi has used artificial intelligence to build more than 200 apps, including a homework-submission platform and a secondhand marketplace. He pitches ideas to real investors, idolises Elon Musk and hopes to become a computer scientist.

Around him, classmates program humanoid robots to play soccer, attend coding workshops and train on flight simulators. Posters across the 30-acre (12-hectare) boarding school campus encourage students to "create a virtual world in five minutes with AI vibe coding."

"In the past, if I couldn't solve a problem at home, I'd have to call my teacher, which increases their workload," Peng said. "But now I can just ask AI to help me learn better. It noticeably improved my learning efficiency."

Rare access granted to Reuters at the $39,000-a-year Beijing New Talent Academy offered a window into China's push to weave AI into education. The school, which serves more than 2,000 students, has built its own digital innovation curriculum covering AI, robotics and programming, and developed a classroom AI model incorporating features from popular Chinese systems.

The academy represents the sharp end of a broader transformation. With almost 200 million students enrolled in primary and secondary education, China is undertaking one of the world's largest AI-assisted learning experiments, with the technology increasingly integrated into teaching nationwide.

By 2030, Beijing wants AI literacy to be universal among schoolchildren. Current broad AI education guidelines state that students should progress from understanding basic concepts in their early years to applying advanced tools and critical-thinking skills in complex projects.

A weeks-long Reuters examination, based on school visits, interviews with more than a dozen educators, parents and experts, and a review of more than 100 academic papers and government procurement records, paints one of the most detailed pictures yet of how AI is reshaping Chinese classrooms. It found a sweeping but uneven effort to build a generation of AI-savvy innovators, with little consensus on what AI literacy means, how it should be taught or measured.

China views the technology as central to its economic future and technological rivalry with the United States, hoping early exposure will nurture the homegrown innovation needed for major breakthroughs.

Beijing's state-led push far outpaces efforts in the West. President Xi Jinping has declared AI education fundamental to reform. By contrast, the US relies on decentralized, nonbinding guidance and lacks dedicated funding or state-level teacher standards, according to Stanford University's 2026 AI Index.

A Reuters review of provincial "AI+ education" blueprints reveals a degree of official coordination unseen elsewhere. Nearly half of China's provinces and municipalities have rolled out binding plans. Shanghai mandates at least 30 hours of annual teaching on AI skills per grade, while the Beijing city government plans to integrate AI into student health monitoring, as well as set up 100 AI pilot demonstration schools. Underscoring its importance, regions including Ningxia and Gansu plan to integrate AI literacy directly into high-stakes school entrance exams by 2027.

The documents also offer an early look at more expansive classroom applications. Beyond coding and tutoring, Guizhou is integrating AI facial recognition and behavioral analysis into classrooms, while Shanghai is deploying systems for mental and physical health monitoring. In Yunnan, 14,000 classrooms are slated to have lessons recorded and analysed by AI, turning Chinese schools into a high-stakes testing ground for the opportunities and risks confronting global education.
As AI spreads through Chinese classrooms, many educators are grappling with how to deploy the technology without reinforcing the rote-learning habits policymakers want to move beyond.

Reuters found starkly different approaches across the country. While some schools encourage students like Peng to build and create with AI, others are focused on using the technology to plug gaps in educational resources.

"Implementation is all over the place," said Ted Mo Chen, chief of staff at Chinese education technology startup ClassIn, adding that few schools he had visited had integrated AI into the curriculum effectively.
China's education ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
CLASSROOMS OF THE FUTURE

Headmaster Liu Wei said only a small minority of students at Beijing New Talent Academy would become AI scientists or engineers. For the rest, the objective is to make AI an everyday tool for learning and creating.

Hundreds of kilometres away in rural Anhui province, Funan County Qinqing High School is using the same technology to solve a problem affluent urban areas in China rarely face: a shortage of qualified teachers.

The school's 4,000 pupils, most of them children of migrant workers, learn core subjects through AI-generated lessons, according to headmaster Yang Tianliang. Students follow personalised classes on tablets, with AI agents posing questions rather than providing answers when they struggle.
"An AI agent doesn't suffer from fatigue, and it never makes a student feel stupid for asking a basic question," Yang said.

The school uses popular Chinese AI models from Alibaba's Qwen, ByteDance and Z.AI to generate text, images, interactive lessons and videos. Yang said it had also introduced small-group projects to encourage greater student interaction.

He credited the approach with helping lift university admission rates from below 60% to 90% in recent years, although Reuters could not independently verify the figures. Yang estimated at least 200 other Chinese schools were experimenting with similar systems.
An Alibaba spokesperson said its open-source AI models and Cloud for Youth Programme give students direct access to AI tools and education. ByteDance and Z.AI did not respond to requests for comment.
Schools such as Funan County Qinqing High School offer a glimpse of how quickly AI is spreading through China's education system.

Since 2024, China's education ministry has encouraged schools to introduce AI courses, train teachers and develop pilot programmes. Primary-school pupils are introduced to basic AI tools, while older students learn how AI systems work and apply them to increasingly sophisticated projects.
A Reuters review of more than 100 government procurement documents found authorities committed at least $31 million in the past year to AI classroom equipment, training and teaching platforms.

The true figure is likely far higher, scattered across thousands of local budgets and not officially tallied. Consultancy iResearch estimates 2025 spending on education digitalisation at just under $83 billion, with generative AI projects accounting for 46% of AI education procurement.
AN EXPERIMENT WITHOUT A CLEAR SCORECARD
China has yet to establish a standard framework for measuring AI literacy, leaving schools to experiment and making success difficult to assess.
"Mature, widely adopted assessment rubrics for compulsory school-level AI competency are still being built," said Selena Guo, portfolio lead at research firm China Policy.

Preliminary research into AI's effects on children's learning also offers mixed signals, with some studies suggesting short-term gains while raising questions about longer-term intellectual development.

A recent study examining nearly 27,000 Chinese teenagers found AI adoption was associated with an 18% increase in homework scores but a 20% decline in monthly examination scores within six months, with the biggest declines in social science subjects.

Another nationwide Chinese survey this year involving more than 320,000 pupils reported educational benefits from AI but also concerns about dependence and weaker independent thinking. Students using AI at least three times weekly showed lower memory, comprehension, analytical and creative skills than less frequent users.

The findings do not establish causation but reinforce teacher concerns about cognitive outsourcing, where children increasingly delegate mental tasks to technology rather than develop those skills themselves.
Chen from ClassIn warned that children's thinking processes could be "completely bypassed" if schools failed to prevent them from relying on AI for quick answers.
Chinese academic research reviewed by Reuters also suggested that students in rural areas may be particularly vulnerable to cognitive outsourcing and device addiction.
FINDING THE RIGHT BALANCE
Some educators and parents are already experimenting with safeguards to keep AI from replacing critical thinking.

At Beijing New Talent Academy, Peng said he tries to solve coding problems himself before asking AI for hints rather than complete answers. He said the technology has helped deepen his understanding of maths.
"I think AI is a tool that helps me, not something I depend on."
For Beijing parent Rita Luan, whose 11-year-old daughter attends a leading public school in the capital, the challenge is ensuring that AI strengthens rather than shortcuts learning.

She said her daughter's school still largely teaches AI concepts rather than practical applications, so she supplements lessons at home, teaching her daughter to prompt ByteDance's Doubao chatbot under close supervision.
Her rule: spend 15 minutes trying to solve a difficult maths problem before turning to AI. Days later, Luan asks her to solve the same problem without help.
"The point is to make sure she actually digested the solution," she said.

news.article_content:
With OpenAI models and Codex, Revolut is giving its teams more room to solve complex problems—from software engineering to financial crime.

Revolut⁠(opens in a new window) was built to challenge the way people interact with money. That ambition now stretches across more than 40 markets, 800,000 businesses and a consumer base that’s grown by 23% in the last 12 months.

Add to that a company culture that expects small, lean teams to move quickly and it’s no surprise that ChatGPT and Codex have proven a natural fit.

“The perfect description for a high-caliber Revolut person is someone who can identify a problem really quickly, deduce the solution, design four scenarios, identify the best one of those four then take it to market,” says Kim Maniovich, Revolut’s Global Head of Business Marketing.

“Partnering with OpenAI enables us to build a lot of these solutions in a way that’s incredibly lean, cost-efficient and really tailored to the unique way that we work.”

But moving faster is only part of the opportunity. For Revolut, the bigger question is what becomes possible when talented people spend less time on the mechanics of getting things done—and more time tackling problems that could fundamentally change financial services.

As Revolut grows, so does the complexity of protecting its customers. According to one report⁠(opens in a new window), over half of adults worldwide reported a scam encounter in 2025.

For Revolut, every transaction creates another opportunity to identify suspicious activity, investigate potential risks and implement robust and tailored protections for its customers. But the sheer volume of those transactions far outstrips the human resources available to any bank.

“The biggest problem we can tackle with AI today is the scaling of humans versus the demand that we get,” says AI Lead David Abitbol. That’s why one of Revolut’s largest AI applications is a FinCrime agent powered by OpenAI models.

Rather than requiring investigators to work through every eligible case manually, the agent can examine information, apply Revolut’s rules and complete the defined process automatically.

The release of GPT‑5.5 was a turning point. It was then, says Abitbol, that the models had become capable and cost-effective enough for Revolut to delegate screening and investigation workflows entirely to the agent. The result is greater capacity to monitor transactions without increasing investigator headcount at the same rate as demand.

That, adds Information Security Engineer Mo Amiri, “translates directly into stronger protection and a more resilient system our customers can trust.”

‘Move fast but build trust’ could easily be Revolut’s internal engineering slogan. While Abitbol points out that Codex has delivered a 30-60% reduction in coding time, he’s also clear that certain guardrails are non-negotiable.

“We have a systematic framework where anyone in the company who’s building anything with AI has the same set of standards across development, A/B testing, and business metric prediction,” he says. “So every engineer is held to the same standard of quality across the company. We started to get enough intelligence for reasonable costs where we could increasingly delegate initial investigations and screenings to the agent.”

For Senior Platform Engineer Dmitry Pitik, that 30-60% reduction in coding time became tangible while he was building an internal code-review service. He designed the system, broke it into features and initially assumed he’d need a development team to implement it.

“I realised I don’t need a whole team of developers to implement this,” he recalls. “I can just launch different agents and assign each of them a particular task.” Codex became his implementation team, while Dmitry spent more time designing the system, planning the work and reviewing what came back.

This is a pattern that Abitbol has seen across Revolut. As Codex returns capacity to engineers they’re using that reclaimed time “to spend more time discussing design and the best solution. So we spend more time designing instead of implementing.”

That doesn’t remove the need for engineering expertise, it just changes where that expertise is applied. “Every developer is responsible for the code they produce, and we don’t blindly trust AI,” Pitik says. The result is a different division of work: AI can help with implementation, while engineers devote more attention to the decisions that determine whether the software is useful, reliable and worth building.

That overhead is worth it. As Codex works on one task, Pitik can work in parallel on another. That kind of multitasking is essential in a company where, as Kim Maniovich explains, the average employee has “three different jobs.” Using Codex creates a virtuous (if challenging) flywheel where “month on month the targets we’re setting get more aggressive, but also more attainable. And so the bar keeps moving up. AI is making that possible.”

Examples of what Revolut has been able to do with this new-found capacity include developing a tool to build web UIs for internal apps and external-facing products.

Or turning seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context in a single day, creating a foundation for tools intended to help designers work more effectively. The exercise illustrates how AI can make accumulated organisational knowledge more accessible, reducing the effort required to work with complex systems. “We can shift focus from the things which are important but hard to do without AI to the things which matter for customers,” says Senior Designer Dmytro Pavlov.

Mo Amiri’s job is to make sure all of this speed is matched by security—not just for customers but for Revolut’s own employees. That gives him two views of AI at once: how it can help Revolut investigate a problem, and what teams need before they can deploy it safely.

In a phishing investigation, for example, an analyst once had to gather an email, inspect its links and attachments, trace the sender and assemble the evidence manually. “With stronger AI tools, we can uncover those connections instantly, and dig deeper into the questions that really matter,” he says.

While AI does the legwork and presents an investigator with a structured case, it’s still down to the individual to review the original records, decide whether the explanation makes sense and approve any action.

Amiri applies the same thinking when teams bring new AI applications into Revolut. He follows the complete chain: what information the system sees, where that information goes, which tools it can reach, what it can do with that access and what happens when something fails. He also tests whether apparently convincing conclusions are actually supported by the evidence.

“The most critical decision is always about accountability,” he says. “If an AI tool suggests a code change, a human engineer needs to understand that change well enough to stand by it. That directly drives how we design the review process, giving developers the context they need without cluttering their everyday workflow.”

For Revolut, safeguards aren’t separate from innovation. They help establish the conditions under which teams can confidently adopt more capable technology. “That’s how you earn real confidence in AI,” he explains, “by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go.”

Start with a problem worth solving. Revolut has put AI to work where demand is growing fastest and the stakes for customers are highest.

Use speed to raise ambition, not lower standards. Time saved on coding and investigation creates room for better design, harder questions and more consequential work.

Keep people on the hook. AI can gather evidence, write code and recommend action. A person still needs to understand the work well enough to stand behind it.

Build trust before you scale. Be clear about what a system can see, what it can do and what happens when it fails—then test those decisions as you go.

Make your knowledge usable. AI works better when it can reach clear, well-organised context. The same exercise often shows where the organisation itself needs to be clearer.

Kim Maniovich connects that future to the culture driving the work. “I hope that we can take the values that we operate by every day—this unapologetic ambition, the desire to never settle—and enable people to apply that to their own lives through the products that we build for them.”

As AI makes it easier to build, the differentiator becomes knowing what to build—and maintaining the judgment, standards and customer understanding to do it well. For Revolut, that’s the bigger promise of intelligence at work: less time spent on the mechanics of getting things done, and more capacity to make financial services safer, simpler and more useful for everyone.

Mo Amiri’s job is to make sure all of this speed is matched by security—not just for customers but for Revolut’s own employees. That gives him two views of AI at once: how it can help Revolut investigate a problem, and what teams need before they can deploy it safely.

In a phishing investigation, for example, an analyst once had to gather an email, inspect its links and attachments, trace the sender and assemble the evidence manually. “With stronger AI tools, we can uncover those connections instantly, and dig deeper into the questions that really matter,” he says.

While AI does the legwork and presents an investigator with a structured case, it’s still down to the individual to review the original records, decide whether the explanation makes sense and approve any action.

Amiri applies the same thinking when teams bring new AI applications into Revolut. He follows the complete chain: what information the system sees, where that information goes, which tools it can reach, what it can do with that access and what happens when something fails. He also tests whether apparently convincing conclusions are actually supported by the evidence.

“The most critical decision is always about accountability,” he says. “If an AI tool suggests a code change, a human engineer needs to understand that change well enough to stand by it. That directly drives how we design the review process, giving developers the context they need without cluttering their everyday workflow.”

For Revolut, safeguards aren’t separate from innovation. They help establish the conditions under which teams can confidently adopt more capable technology. “That’s how you earn real confidence in AI,” he explains, “by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go.”

Start with a problem worth solving. Revolut has put AI to work where demand is growing fastest and the stakes for customers are highest.

Use speed to raise ambition, not lower standards. Time saved on coding and investigation creates room for better design, harder questions and more consequential work.

Keep people on the hook. AI can gather evidence, write code and recommend action. A person still needs to understand the work well enough to stand behind it.

Build trust before you scale. Be clear about what a system can see, what it can do and what happens when it fails—then test those decisions as you go.

Make your knowledge usable. AI works better when it can reach clear, well-organised context. The same exercise often shows where the organisation itself needs to be clearer.

Kim Maniovich connects that future to the culture driving the work. “I hope that we can take the values that we operate by every day—this unapologetic ambition, the desire to never settle—and enable people to apply that to their own lives through the products that we build for them.”

As AI makes it easier to build, the differentiator becomes knowing what to build—and maintaining the judgment, standards and customer understanding to do it well. For Revolut, that’s the bigger promise of intelligence at work: less time spent on the mechanics of getting things done, and more capacity to make financial services safer, simpler and more useful for everyone.

news.article_content_zh:
借助 OpenAI 模型和 Codex，Revolut 为其团队提供了更多空间来解决从软件工程到金融犯罪的复杂问题。

Revolut⁠（在新窗口中打开）旨在挑战人们与金钱互动的方式。这一雄心现已覆盖 40 多个市场、80 万家企业以及过去 12 个月增长了 23% 的消费者群。

再加上公司文化要求小型、精干的团队能够快速行动，因此事实证明 ChatGPT 和 Codex 是天生的搭档也就不足为奇了。

Revolut 全球业务营销主管 Kim Maniovich 表示：“对高素质 Revolut 人员的完美描述是能够快速识别问题、推断解决方案、设计四种方案、确定这四种方案中最好的一种，然后将其推向市场。”

“与 OpenAI 合作使我们能够以极其精简、经济高效且真正适合我们独特工作方式的方式构建许多此类解决方案。”

但更快的行动只是机遇的一部分。对于 Revolut 来说，更大的问题是，当有才华的人花更少的时间在完成工作的机制上，而花更多的时间来解决可能从根本上改变金融服务的问题时，会发生什么。

随着 Revolut 的发展，保护客户的复杂性也随之增加。根据一份报告（在新窗口中打开），全球超过一半的成年人报告称在 2025 年遭遇过诈骗。

对于 Revolut 来说，每笔交易都会创造另一个机会来识别可疑活动、调查潜在风险并为其客户实施强大且量身定制的保护。但这些交易的绝对数量远远超出了任何银行可用的人力资源。

人工智能负责人戴维·阿比特博尔 (David Abitbol) 表示：“当今人工智能可以解决的最大问题是人类的规模与我们所获得的需求之间的关系。”这就是为什么 Revolut 最大的人工智能应用程序之一是由 OpenAI 模型支持的 FinCrime 代理。

代理可以检查信息、应用 Revolut 规则并自动完成定义的流程，而不是要求调查人员手动处理每个符合条件的案件。

GPT-5.5 的发布是一个转折点。 Abitbol 表示，就在那时，这些模型已经变得足够强大且具有成本效益，Revolut 可以将筛选和调查工作流程完全委托给代理。其结果是，在不按需求增加调查员人数的情况下，监控交易的能力得到提高。

信息安全工程师 Mo Amiri 补充道，“这直接转化为我们的客户可以信赖的更强大的保护和更具弹性的系统。”

“快速行动，但建立信任”很容易成为 Revolut 的内部工程口号。虽然 Abitbol 指出 Codex 已将编码时间缩短了 30-60%，但他也明确指出某些护栏是不容协商的。

“我们有一个系统框架，公司中使用人工智能构建任何东西的任何人在开发、A/B 测试和业务指标预测方面都拥有相同的一套标准，”他说。 “因此，整个公司的每位工程师都必须遵守相同的质量标准。我们开始以合理的成本获得足够的情报，从而可以将初步调查和筛查越来越多地委托给代理。”

news.title: Data centre construction stocks lose $4.2tn as boom in AI trade unravels
news.title_en: Data centre construction stocks lose $4.2tn as boom in AI trade unravels

inline_images.alt: Data centre construction stocks lose $4.2tn as boom in AI trade unravels
Data centre construction stocks lose $4.2tn as boom in AI trade unravels
Data centre construction stocks lose $4.2tn as boom in AI trade unravels

news.author: Clara Murray
news.article_content:
Global manufacturing, utility and mining companies have shed $4.2tn in value since June as the AI “picks and shovels” trade swings into reverse.

Companies more frequently linked by media coverage to data centre construction have been hit hardest by the sell-off, an FT analysis found, as investors’ confidence in the AI boom wobbles.

The losses wiped out almost half of the $9.4tn in value that the same companies gained in the previous 12 months as investors piled into the manufacturers of everything from jet engines adapted to power hyperscale data centres to the advanced fibre optics needed to connect AI server racks.

Caterpillar, a leading supplier of gas generators to data centres, has seen its market capitalisation slashed by $214bn, or 44 per cent, since its shares hit an all-time high on June 30, according to FactSet data.

Nuclear power company Oklo plunged 49 per cent despite signing a contract with Meta in January. Comfort Systems, which makes HVAC systems, and Corning, a fibre optics manufacturer, both lost around half of their value over the same period.

Paul Kedrosky, a venture capitalist and fellow at the MIT Institute, said investors had been wrong to start treating old-school industrial firms like semiconductor stocks. “It had become endless in discussions with hedge funds and family offices, this idea that everything was now a growth stock — which is ludicrous, of course.”

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The sell-off comes amid wider market turmoil for AI-related shares, as investors question whether escalating debt-financed capital expenditures at hyperscalers and mounting political opposition to data centres in the US could lead to a bust.

That has hit industrial groups whose fortunes are increasingly bound to the build-out. The sector has been the second-worst-performing in the S&P 500 since the summer, after technology.

“There has been a lot of institutional investment piling blindly into these trades that probably fuelled an overly enthusiastic valuation on some of these [companies],” said Brett Ryan, senior US economist at Deutsche Bank.

The stock market was “finally benchmarking to what credit was already telling you” about the growth in risky financing for data centre construction, he added.

However, others argue that the companies supplying the boom were on solid foundations, with demand still vastly outstripping supply. Spending on data centre construction — excluding IT equipment and chips — hit $96bn in the US in the 12 months to September, the latest government data showed.

“In terms of the fundamentals of revenues and the potential earnings for these companies, we are still looking at a very strong prospect,” said Alex Cordovil, an analyst at Dell’Oro Group.

Wider trends such as electrification and supply chain restructuring continued to support many industrial firms’ core businesses. “The build-out is not decelerating as of yet . . . backlogs are at record highs, meaning that until 2027 . . . revenue growth is already baked in,” he added.

Richard S Warzala, chief executive of Allient, an industrial controls maker, said demand for AI was not going to decline. “They can have a moratorium on new data centre installation, but those that are already started need to be completed,” he said in an earnings call on November 5.

Third-quarter results showed strong demand. Many gas turbine manufacturers said they were taking billions of dollars in orders in the first nine months of 2026. Caterpillar reported a record $78bn backlog and said its power generation sales grew 75 per cent year-on-year, driven by data centre demand.

Siemens’ backlog of orders for its electrical equipment from data centres grew 60 per cent in 2026 to €7bn, while Eaton, which also supplies electrics, reported orders had doubled year-on-year.

Kedrosky cautioned that backlogs and orders were trailing indicators reflecting expectations, with people “double and triple ordering to protect their position in the queue given perceived scarcity”.

The impact of the data centre moratoriums and restrictions widely backed by US voters in this month’s midterm elections is still unclear.

Citi researchers said in a note published after the elections that while they expected tighter regulations to bring more volatility to the data centre industry, widespread restrictions on construction remained unlikely.

Joseph Dominguez of Constellation Energy told investors that the market movement following the election had been an “overreaction” and Democrats “care very deeply” about protecting blue-collar jobs at data centres.

Others say any bans would just shift construction to more friendly jurisdictions.

“At the end of the day, if there is demand for these things, they will get built somewhere,” said Deutsche Bank’s Ryan.

news.article_content_zh:
自 6 月份以来，随着人工智能“镐和铲”贸易的逆转，全球制造、公用事业和采矿公司的价值已减少 4.2 兆美元。

英国《金融时报》分析发现，随着投资者对人工智能热潮的信心动摇，那些经常被媒体报道与数据中心建设联系在一起的公司受到抛售的打击最为严重。

这些损失几乎抹去了这些公司在过去 12 个月中获得的 9.4 万亿美元价值的一半，因为投资者纷纷涌入这些制造商，从适合为超大规模数据中心供电的喷气发动机到连接人工智能服务器机架所需的先进光纤。

根据 FactSet 数据，卡特彼勒是数据中心燃气发电机的领先供应商，自 6 月 30 日股价创下历史新高以来，其市值已缩水 2140 亿美元，即 44%。

尽管核电公司 Oklo 在 1 月份与 Meta 签署了合同，但股价仍暴跌 49%。制造暖通空调系统的舒适系统公司和光纤制造商康宁公司的价值同期都损失了大约一半。

风险投资家、麻省理工学院研究员保罗·凯德罗斯基 (Paul Kedrosky) 表示，投资者开始将传统工业公司视为半导体股票，这是错误的。 “与对冲基金和家族办公室的讨论变得无休无止，这种认为现在一切都是成长型股票的想法——当然，这是荒谬的。”

此次抛售正值人工智能相关股票出现更广泛的市场动荡，因为投资者质疑超大规模企业债务融资资本支出的不断增加以及对美国数据中心的政治反对是否会导致破产。

这对工业集团造成了打击，它们的命运越来越依赖于扩建。自夏季以来，该行业一直是标准普尔 500 指数中表现第二差的行业，仅次于科技行业。

德意志银行高级美国经济学家布雷特·瑞安（Brett Ryan）表示：“大量机构投资盲目涌入这些交易，可能导致对其中一些公司的估值过于热情。”

他补充称，对于数据中心建设风险融资的增长，股市“终于在参照信贷已经告诉你的情况”。

然而，其他人认为，提供繁荣的公司基础坚实，需求仍然远远超过供应。最新的政府数据显示，在截至9月份的12个月中，美国数据中心建设支出（不包括IT设备和芯片）达到960亿美元。

戴尔奥罗集团（Dell 'Oro Group）分析师亚历克斯·科多维尔（Alex Cordovil）表示：“就这些公司的收入基本面和潜在盈利而言，我们仍然看好非常强劲的前景。”

电气化和供应链重组等更广泛的趋势继续支持许多工业企业的核心业务。“到目前为止，扩建还没有减速……积压订单处于历史高位，这意味着直到2027年……收入增长已经被消化了。”

花旗研究人员在选举后发布的一份报告中表示，虽然他们预计更严格的监管将给数据中心行业带来更大的波动性，但大范围限制建设的可能性仍然不大。

Constellation Energy的Joseph Dominguez对投资者表示，大选后的市场波动是一种“过度反应”，民主党人“非常关心”保护数据中心的蓝领工作岗位。

还有人表示，任何禁令只会将建设转向更友好的地区。

paragraphs: Global manufacturing, utility and mining companies have shed $4.2tn in value since June as the AI “picks and shovels” trade swings into reverse.
Companies more frequently linked by media coverage to data centre construction have been hit hardest by the sell-off, an FT analysis found, as investors’ confidence in the AI boom wobbles.

The losses wiped out almost half of the $9.4tn in value that the same companies gained in the previous 12 months as investors piled into the manufacturers of everything from jet engines adapted to power hyperscale data centres to the advanced fibre optics needed to connect AI server racks.

Caterpillar, a leading supplier of gas generators to data centres, has seen its market capitalisation slashed by $214bn, or 44 per cent, since its shares hit an all-time high on June 30, according to FactSet data.

Nuclear power company Oklo plunged 49 per cent despite signing a contract with Meta in January. Comfort Systems, which makes HVAC systems, and Corning, a fibre optics manufacturer, both lost around half of their value over the same period.

Paul Kedrosky, a venture capitalist and fellow at the MIT Institute, said investors had been wrong to start treating old-school industrial firms like semiconductor stocks. “It had become endless in discussions with hedge funds and family offices, this idea that everything was now a growth stock — which is ludicrous, of course.”
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The sell-off comes amid wider market turmoil for AI-related shares, as investors question whether escalating debt-financed capital expenditures at hyperscalers and mounting political opposition to data centres in the US could lead to a bust.
That has hit industrial groups whose fortunes are increasingly bound to the build-out. The sector has been the second-worst-performing in the S&P 500 since the summer, after technology.

“There has been a lot of institutional investment piling blindly into these trades that probably fuelled an overly enthusiastic valuation on some of these [companies],” said Brett Ryan, senior US economist at Deutsche Bank.
The stock market was “finally benchmarking to what credit was already telling you” about the growth in risky financing for data centre construction, he added.

However, others argue that the companies supplying the boom were on solid foundations, with demand still vastly outstripping supply. Spending on data centre construction — excluding IT equipment and chips — hit $96bn in the US in the 12 months to September, the latest government data showed.
“In terms of the fundamentals of revenues and the potential earnings for these companies, we are still looking at a very strong prospect,” said Alex Cordovil, an analyst at Dell’Oro Group.

Wider trends such as electrification and supply chain restructuring continued to support many industrial firms’ core businesses. “The build-out is not decelerating as of yet . . . backlogs are at record highs, meaning that until 2027 . . . revenue growth is already baked in,” he added.

Richard S Warzala, chief executive of Allient, an industrial controls maker, said demand for AI was not going to decline. “They can have a moratorium on new data centre installation, but those that are already started need to be completed,” he said in an earnings call on November 5.

Third-quarter results showed strong demand. Many gas turbine manufacturers said they were taking billions of dollars in orders in the first nine months of 2026. Caterpillar reported a record $78bn backlog and said its power generation sales grew 75 per cent year-on-year, driven by data centre demand.
Siemens’ backlog of orders for its electrical equipment from data centres grew 60 per cent in 2026 to €7bn, while Eaton, which also supplies electrics, reported orders had doubled year-on-year.
Kedrosky cautioned that backlogs and orders were trailing indicators reflecting expectations, with people “double and triple ordering to protect their position in the queue given perceived scarcity”.
The impact of the data centre moratoriums and restrictions widely backed by US voters in this month’s midterm elections is still unclear.

Citi researchers said in a note published after the elections that while they expected tighter regulations to bring more volatility to the data centre industry, widespread restrictions on construction remained unlikely.

Joseph Dominguez of Constellation Energy told investors that the market movement following the election had been an “overreaction” and Democrats “care very deeply” about protecting blue-collar jobs at data centres.
Others say any bans would just shift construction to more friendly jurisdictions.
“At the end of the day, if there is demand for these things, they will get built somewhere,” said Deutsche Bank’s Ryan.

news.author: Jackie Snow
news.article_content:
Floating data centers? A Dallas startup bets on a new approach for a controversial industry Trevor Bach September 26, 2026 8 min read Dallas startup Mousterian is planning to put its data centers on water to help with cooling and water usage. (Photo

But those data centers, which sometimes occupy hundreds of acres and use the resource equivalent of small cities, are located on land, often near people's homes. A Dallas startup, called Mousterian, is taking a different approach: Developing data centers that float on water.

The unique design, said Min Suh, Mousterian's CEO and cofounder, allows the floating data centers avoid municipal water supplies entirely, because they use the surrounding body of water as part of a closed-loop cooling system. The floating data centers also don't make noise and are ideally located near power plants, so they can access energy easily and avoid bothering residents, because people generally aren't living in such heavy industrial zones anyway.

"We like to think, 'If we are going to build a data center, we're trying to do it in the most sustainable way possible,' " said Suh.

Now several years into an AI-driven construction boom, the United States is home to over 4,000 data centers, including more than 1,000 hyperscalers, the largest facilities. Many of the biggest are in Texas, including Stargate, a potentially $500 billion joint venture in Abilene led by OpenAI, and Frontier, an incoming 1,200-acre project in Shackelford County. Numerous projects are also underway in data center-heavy D-FW, which was recently ranked by Cushman and Wakefield as the top primary data center market in the Americas.

The boom has created a rush of Texas construction jobs and been welcomed by many political and business leaders. "I think of [data centers] almost like the highways and the airports that are the fundamental infrastructure of the future," Dallas Regional Chamber executive Mike Rosa told The News last year.

But the computing centers' vast energy and water consumption — the biggest culprit is their cooling systems — has emerged as a persistent flashpoint, prompting community outrage and various local and state moratoriums.

In Texas, Abbott's new moratorium mandates an audit of pending data center projects that includes details on their cooling systems and impact on local water supplies, and politicians including Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico, the state's Democratic gubernatorial and U.S. Senate candidates, are also loudly calling for tighter water regulations.

One controversial project — a planned data center about 60 miles southeast of Dallas that was expected to pull millions of gallons of water per day from Cedar Creek Lake, which also supplies drinking water for Fort Worth — was already scrapped.

"We're killing ourselves letting the data centers in," said Ashley Cook, a lawyer who led the fight against the project. "You're basically turning a rural residential peaceful community into an industrial corridor."

Some industry leaders have pushed back against the water-guzzling stigma, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who has called the water issue "totally fake" even while pushing for more renewable energy use. Experts say the consumption issues are in fact relatively nuanced and localized. Each facility's design and technology is also important.

Yet as the world's seemingly insatiable demand for computing power keeps rising, developers have also been exploring more novel solutions. Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, among others, have unveiled plans for data centers in space. Earlier this year, a wind-powered, underwater data center began operating several miles off the coast of Shanghai. In Norway, a data center complex was built into an abandoned mine, with seawater-based cooling from an adjacent fjord.

Several years ago, a California-based company called Nautilus Data Technologies developed the world's first floating data center, which it built atop a refurbished, 700-ton barge in the San Joaquin River at the industrial Port of Stockton. The two-story operation, which resembles a white shipping container, began operating in 2021 with a cooling system that cycles around 4,500 gallons of river water per minute, with screens that serve as filters to keep fish and plants out of the intake system.

The site proved more ecologically sustainable, with far lower electricity and operating costs than typical land-based operations, according to Nautilus. It was also well received by local officials, and attracted San Joaquin County as an anchor tenant.

For some of its developers, it also served as a launching pad: "Taking those lessons of building the first floating data center," said Suh, "we kind of took all the best components of different technologies available and basically created this new company."

Suh, who has extensive data center experience but was not involved with the California floating data center project, cofounded Mousterian — the name refers to the Middle Paleolithic era, when humans first started using complex tools — with Chase Ott-Wick, a former senior engineer on the California project, and Gabe Andrews, another data center veteran and former Nautilus executive.

The 10-person company, which is self-funded and quietly launched last year, is based in downtown Dallas and handles data center design, engineering and development. In addition to floating data centers, it also develops land-based and water-adjacent facilities — Suh said it's best to characterize the company as "a high-performance data center developer with unique facility offerings versus a purely floating data center company" — but is broadly focused on delivering projects that require far less energy and don't use municipal groundwater.

"A lot of the tech companies and hyperscalers were still maybe 10 to 15 years behind on how they were developing and delivering data centers," said Suh, who also pointed to conspicuous examples of companies building water-guzzling facilities in dry areas like the American West. "And so we're trying to push the envelope the opposite way, by being kind of very water sensitive."

The startup has already landed major institutional partners: Earlier this year, in its highest-profile move yet, Mousterian signed an agreement with Samsung Heavy Industries, one of the world's largest shipbuilders, which last month led to an engineering contract to jointly develop a fleet of floating data centers.

Under the terms of the deal, Mousterian and the Korean manufacturing giant are co-designing the vessels, which will be manufactured by Samsung in South Korea and then shipped and finished by Mousterian likely in Texas or Louisiana. Mousterian is also designing the facilities' internal equipment.

The floating data centers will have about a one-acre footprint and a capacity of about 50 megawatts, which roughly qualifies them as large data centers. (Stargate, the massive Abilene project, is designed for a capacity of up to 1,200 megawatts.)

The plan is for the new floating fleet to be deployed in different locations around the U.S. Mousterian currently has a half dozen different project sites — featuring a mix of floating and land-based designs — in various stages, including a hybrid floating and land-based campus next to a power plant in Houston and what it's calling "a large-scale floating campus" in the San Jose, Calif. area.

Suh declined to provide more details about the other projects' locations, but the floating data centers are typically located in sites like deep river harbors or shipping channels, where they're moored close enough to land so that employees can easily walk back and forth between the floating facility and complementary land-based facilities.

"Within 30 seconds, you know, you're in a regular air-conditioned office, with a bathroom and kitchen," Suh said.

The data centers will also source energy that's not connected to the public grid, while their pass-through water cooling systems will help give them a Power Usage Effectiveness, or PUE, score of 1.15 or 1.2, Suh said, which would rank among the industry's best. Traditional data centers' PUE scores, where 1.0 indicates perfect energy efficiency, are typically 1.5 or higher.

The floating data center concept has its complications, said Ed Hirs, an energy economist at the University of Houston, including a potentially high development cost, the access to large power sources and even environmental issues, if the warmer water discharging back into the water source disrupts marine life.

"It's all a matter of how much money they want to spend," Hirs said.

Another major challenge is identifying the right locations, because of the very specific requirements needed to make the projects work. But being an industry innovator also has its benefits.

"It's just that we're the only company looking for these sites right now," Suh said, "so we've kind of had our pick."
